payload.stem: A researcher takes independent random samples of customers who receive a coupon and of customers who do not receive a coupon, and records whether each one make a second purchase. Let $p_1$ be the proportion of all customers who receive a coupon who make a second purchase, and let $p_2$ be the proportion of all customers who do not receive a coupon who make a second purchase. The researcher suspects that $p_1$ is greater than $p_2$ and will carry out a test of significance. Which of the following gives the appropriate hypotheses?

options.why: The alternative hypothesis points in the direction opposite to the researcher's suspicion.
The researcher suspects that $p_1$ is greater than $p_2$, so the alternative hypothesis is one-sided in that direction and the null hypothesis states no difference between the population proportions.
Uses a two-sided alternative although the researcher suspects a difference in one specific direction.
States the hypotheses with sample proportions; hypotheses are about the population proportions, not the statistics.

verification.independent_path: each option differs from the key by exactly one named defect: the direction, the use of statistics, or a two-sided alternative

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is $H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0$ and $H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0$. The researcher suspects that $p_1$ is greater than $p_2$, so the alternative hypothesis is one-sided in that direction and the null hypothesis states no difference between the population proportions.
$H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0$ and $H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0$ is incorrect: The alternative hypothesis points in the direction opposite to the researcher's suspicion.
$H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0$ and $H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0$ is incorrect: Uses a two-sided alternative although the researcher suspects a difference in one specific direction.
$H_0: \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0$ and $H_a: \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > 0$ is incorrect: States the hypotheses with sample proportions; hypotheses are about the population proportions, not the statistics.

payload.stem: A seed company claims that $80\%$ of its seeds germinate. In a random sample of $50$ seeds, $36$ seeds germinated, and the researcher suspects that the proportion of all seeds that germinate is less than $0.8$. To test the claim, a computer simulated $50$ random samples of $50$ seeds when the true proportion is $0.8$. The dotplot shown gives the number in each simulated sample. Using the simulation and a significance level of $0.05$, which of the following is the best conclusion? (Estimate the P-value to two decimal places.)

stimulus.description: Dotplot of 50 simulated sample counts when the null hypothesis is true

data.title: Simulated number of seeds out of 50 when the claim is true

options.text: The estimated P-value is $0.90$, which is greater than $0.05$, so there is not convincing evidence that the proportion of all seeds that germinate is less than $0.8$.
options.why: Counts the simulated values on the wrong side of the observed value, which is the opposite tail from the alternative hypothesis.

options.text: The estimated P-value is $0.10$, which is greater than $0.05$, so there is not convincing evidence that the proportion of all seeds that germinate is less than $0.8$.
options.why: 5 of the 50 simulated counts are as extreme as the observed value in the direction of $H_a$, so the estimated P-value is $5/50 = 0.10$, and comparing it with $0.05$ gives the decision.

options.text: The estimated P-value is $0.10$, which is the probability that the null hypothesis is true, so the claim of $0.8$ is likely to be true.
options.why: Interprets the P-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true; it is the probability of results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true.

options.text: The estimated P-value is $0.10$, which is greater than $0.05$, so there is convincing evidence that the proportion of all seeds that germinate is less than $0.8$.
options.why: Finds the P-value correctly but reverses the decision rule: a P-value below the significance level is evidence against the null hypothesis.

payload.stem: A researcher constructs a $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of apples in an orchard that have a blemish. The researcher then constructs a $90\%$ confidence interval from a new random sample that is $2$ times as large, and the sample proportion is about the same. The margin of error of the new interval is about what percent of the margin of error of the original interval?

options.text: About $42\%$ of the original margin of error
options.why: Divides by $2$ instead of by $\sqrt{2}$ when the sample size changes; the margin of error is proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$.

options.text: About $59\%$ of the original margin of error
options.why: The margin of error is proportional to $z^*/\sqrt{n}$; the critical value changes by a factor of about $0.839$ and the sample size changes by a factor of $2$, so the margin changes by $0.839/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.59$.

options.text: About $71\%$ of the original margin of error
options.why: Accounts only for the change in the sample size and ignores the change in the confidence level.

options.text: About $84\%$ of the original margin of error
options.why: Accounts only for the change in the confidence level and ignores the change in the sample size.

parts.label: A

payload.title: A battery: a single value, a sample mean and a confidence interval

stimulus.description: The package of each battery says that it lasts $40$ hours. The manufacturer reports that the lifetime of a battery produced by a production line is approximately normally distributed with mean $41$ hours and standard deviation $4$ hours. An inspector who does not rely on the report selects a random sample of $25$ batteries from a large production run and finds a sample mean of $42$ hours and a sample standard deviation of $4$ hours. For a $95\%$ confidence interval with $24$ degrees of freedom, $t^* = 2.064$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: What is the probability that a randomly selected battery has a value of less than $39$ hours? Round to three decimal places.

rubric_rows.criterion: Standardizes the value: $z = (39 - 41)/4 \approx -0.50$
common_errors: divides by the wrong standard deviation
subtracts in the wrong order

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the probability from the normal distribution (answer 0.309)
common_errors: finds the upper tail

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: A random sample of $25$ batteries is selected. State the mean and the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar x$.
parts.model_answer: The mean is $41$ hours and the standard deviation is $4/\sqrt{25} = 0.800$ hours.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean is 41
common_errors: gives the sample mean of the other sample

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the standard deviation of the sampling distribution as $4/\sqrt{25} \approx 0.800$
common_errors: uses the population standard deviation without dividing by the square root of n

payload.stem: A researcher wants to estimate the proportion of households with a vegetable garden among the 480 households in a village and has a complete list of the households. The sample size will be $50$. Which of the following plans is most likely to give an estimate that is not biased?

options.text: Post the survey on the village's website and use the answers of the households that choose to respond.
options.why: Volunteers or respondents who choose to reply can differ from the whole population, so the estimate can be biased.

options.text: Survey the first $50$ households that the researcher meets while walking along the main street.
options.why: Selecting the individuals who are easiest to reach leaves out the others and tends to give a biased estimate.

options.text: Number the households on the list from $1$ to $480$, use a random number generator to choose $50$ different numbers, and survey those households.
options.why: Every individual on the complete list has the same chance of being chosen, so the sample tends to represent the whole population.

options.text: Ask the village council to choose $50$ households that it considers typical of the village.
options.why: Selecting individuals that someone considers typical introduces the chooser's judgment and does not give every individual a chance.

payload.title: Regression of sales on advertising spending: reading computer output

stimulus.description: Computer output for a least-squares regression of sales on advertising spending.

output.title: Regression Analysis: Sales versus advertising spending

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A researcher uses data from $30$ stores to model the relationship between advertising spending ($x$, in thousand dollars) and sales ($y$, in thousand units). The values of $x$ in the data range from $3$ to $14$ thousand dollars. The computer output shown gives the results of a least-squares regression. (i) Write the equation of the least-squares regression line. (ii) Interpret the $y$-intercept of the line in context, and explain whether this interpretation is meaningful.
parts.model_answer: (i) $\hat y = 19.29 + 2.65x$. (ii) When the advertising spending is $0$, the predicted sales is 19.29 thousand units. This is not meaningful, because $0$ is outside the range of the data (3 to 14 thousand dollars), so the interpretation would be an extrapolation.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the equation with the intercept 19.29 and the slope 2.65, in the form $\hat y = 19.29 + 2.65x$

payload.stem: The true value of the proportion of all voters in a city who support a measure is $0.4$. A researcher compares four estimators by simulating $1000$ samples for each and computing the estimate from every sample. The table shown gives the mean and the standard deviation of the estimates for each estimator. Which estimator is best for estimating the true value?

stimulus.description: Mean and standard deviation of the estimates from 1000 simulated samples

data.title: Results of 1000 simulated samples for each estimator

options.text: Estimator C, because the center of its sampling distribution is at the true value.
options.why: Considers bias alone; another estimator is also centered at the true value and has less variability.

options.text: Estimator D, because the center of its sampling distribution is at the true value and its spread is the smallest among the estimators that are centered there.
options.why: An estimator that is unbiased has a sampling distribution centered at the parameter, and among unbiased estimators the one with the least variability is best.

options.text: Estimator A, because it has the smallest spread of all the estimators.
options.why: Considers variability alone; the center of this sampling distribution is not at the true value, so the estimator is biased.

options.text: Estimator B, because its sampling distribution has the largest spread and so covers the most possible values.
options.why: Treats a larger spread as an advantage; more variability means estimates that are farther from the parameter more often.
